opus-5.5.text:
Well, the thing I've learned to look at is not the headline qubit count. Every few months someone announces a chip with more qubits than the last one, and journalists dutifully report it, but the number of physical qubits by itself tells you almost nothing. What matters is the quality of those qubits: how well can you initialize them, operate on them, entangle them, and measure them, and with what error rate.

The key milestone, the one that a lot of us in the field have been watching for, is getting the physical error rates below the threshold where quantum error correction actually starts helping you rather than hurting you. The theory of fault-tolerance, going back to the mid-1990s, says that if your gates are good enough, roughly 99.9% fidelity give or take depending on the code, then you can encode one logical qubit across many physical qubits, and as you make the code bigger, the logical error rate goes down exponentially. That's the whole ballgame. Below threshold, scaling is "just" an engineering problem. Above threshold, adding more qubits just adds more noise.

So when I evaluate a claim, I ask: have they demonstrated a logical qubit that's actually better than the best physical qubit it's made from? When they increase the code distance, does the logical error rate actually drop, and by how much? Can they do logical gates, not just store a logical qubit in memory? Can they do mid-circuit measurement and fast classical feedback, which you need for error correction to work in real time? We've seen genuinely exciting progress on these over the last couple of years, from Google with superconducting qubits, from Quantinuum and others with trapped ions, from groups working with neutral atoms. That's the kind of progress I take seriously.

The other thing I'm always looking for, frankly, is whether a claimed advantage survives scrutiny from classical simulation people. When there's a "quantum supremacy" experiment, I want to see whether the best classical algorithms, which people keep improving, can catch up. Some claims have held up well; others got knocked down. So progress for me means: lower error rates, demonstrated error correction that scales, and claims of advantage that remain standing after the skeptics have had their shot at them. Not press releases.

r002.rationale: It explains that below-threshold physical error rates let error correction reduce logical errors as the code grows, without requiring physical errors to reach zero.

r003.rationale: It says that below threshold, scaling becomes “just” an engineering problem.

r004.rationale: It contrasts below-threshold engineering with above-threshold noise, but does not characterize further qubit increases as a matter of cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I try not to judge it by press releases. The metric I actually care about is pretty boring: how much has the error rate per gate come down, and can you demonstrate error correction where adding more physical qubits makes the logical qubit better rather than worse? That second thing is the whole ballgame. For decades the question was whether you could get below the fault-tolerance threshold at all, and now we've seen experiments, from Google and others, where a bigger surface code genuinely outperforms a smaller one. That's a qualitative shift. It means the thing people like me were arguing about in the early 2000s, whether nature would let you do this, has basically been settled in the affirmative.

The second thing I look at is whether the claims survive the classical skeptics. Every time someone announces a "quantum advantage" experiment, there's a very healthy process where people with big classical computers and clever tensor network methods try to spoil it. Sometimes they succeed, and that's fine, that's how it's supposed to work. What I find encouraging is that the gap has been getting harder to close, not easier. When the classical simulation cost keeps going up faster than the experimentalists' cost, that's a real signal.

What I try to resist is the two failure modes that dominate the discourse. One is the hype mode, where every year is the year quantum computing cures cancer and breaks all encryption. The other is the reflexive dismissal, where people say it's all vaporware. The honest answer is somewhere in between and it's more interesting than either. We have devices with a few hundred to a couple thousand noisy qubits. We don't yet have the millions of physical qubits you'd need to run Shor's algorithm on a cryptographically relevant key. But the roadmap from here to there no longer requires a miracle, it requires engineering, and engineering is a thing humans turn out to be reasonably good at when there's enough money behind it.

So if you ask me for a number, I'd say: watch the logical error rate, watch the number of logical qubits that can be entangled with each other, and watch whether the useful application claims hold up to adversarial scrutiny. When those three things all move in the right direction at once, that's progress. Everything else is marketing.

astra-6.text:
I would look less at the raw number of qubits and more at whether you can actually protect quantum information as you scale up. Qubits are noisy. The central challenge is quantum error correction: encoding a logical qubit into many physical qubits so that you can detect and correct errors without destroying the computation.

The crucial question is, as you make that encoding larger, does the logical error rate go down? And can you preserve that improvement while performing operations between logical qubits? That’s much more informative than simply announcing a device with more qubits.

There are also different milestones. Demonstrating a quantum computation that’s hard to simulate classically is an important scientific achievement. But it doesn’t by itself mean you have a useful, scalable quantum computer. For that, you need a credible path to long computations with reliable logical qubits, and you need to account for the overhead required to get there.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to look at error correction. The central question is whether, as you add more physical qubits and do more error correction, you can make the logical qubits—the qubits that actually store the information—more reliable. Can you demonstrate that the errors go down systematically as you increase the size of the code?

Just counting qubits doesn’t tell you very much. You also need to know how noisy they are, how well you can control them, and whether you can perform operations on the encoded information without losing the protection. A convincing demonstration of quantum advantage is an important milestone, but it’s different from having a scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computer. What I want to see is a clear path from a small demonstration to a machine that can run a long computation reliably.
